**Wells Fargo makes customers liable for all AI agent transactions**

*Updated terms of service expose a gap in open banking consent frameworks that programmes such as PSD3 and the FCA's planned agentic finance standards will need to address as agentic commerce scales.*

Wells Fargo has updated its terms of service to make customers legally responsible for every transaction initiated by an AI agent acting on their behalf. The change applies regardless of whether the customer explicitly authorised the specific payment, shifting all risk from the bank to the consumer in a category of transactions that no existing regulatory framework fully contemplates.

No current open banking standard includes a mechanism for a customer to grant an agent permission to execute a narrowly scoped action, such as paying a specific bill and nothing else. The absence of granular consent frameworks means banks face a binary choice: block AI agents entirely, as JPMorgan Chase did in October, or permit them and disclaim liability, as Wells Fargo has now done. Neither approach is sustainable as agentic commerce matures.

Regulatory thinking is further ahead in Europe. The Financial Conduct Authority announced on October 19 that it would develop a trusted framework for agentic finance collaboratively with industry and other regulators, and EMVCo has drafted a card-based agentic payments standard. But the Wells Fargo move underscores how quickly commercial reality is outpacing regulatory design. The question of who bears liability when an agent acts beyond its intended scope is no longer theoretical for open banking providers building agent-initiated payment flows in Europe.

*Sources: [Wells Fargo Just Made You Legally Responsible for Every Transaction Your AI Agent Makes](https://www.techtimes.com/articles/329947/20261103/wells-fargo-just-made-you-legally-responsible-every-transaction-your-ai-agent-makes.htm) — Techtimes*

**Wandhoefer warns AI agents could make payment authentication obsolete**

*Existing strong customer authentication models were designed for human users and have no adequate answer for autonomous software agents initiating payments at scale.*

Ruth Wandhoefer, one of the payments industry's most prominent regulatory voices, has warned that AI agents could render traditional payment authentication frameworks obsolete. Speaking at an industry event, she argued that strong customer authentication as currently designed assumes a human is present at the point of transaction, an assumption that breaks down when autonomous agents initiate payments on a user's behalf.

Wandhoefer suggested that agentic AI could accelerate the adoption of open finance by enabling automated financial management and lending decisions, but only if the infrastructure adapts. The challenge is not just technical but legal: current European regulations tie authentication to individual consent at the moment of payment, and delegating that consent to a software agent raises questions that neither PSD2 nor the forthcoming PSD3 framework has resolved.

The warning lands as the agentic payments space is moving rapidly from proof-of-concept to early production. Visa and Mastercard have completed live agentic transactions in 2026, Blik has piloted its first agentic payment, and several European banks have run their own trials. An industry alliance with over 25 founding members launched in August. Wandhoefer's point is that the plumbing is being built before the rules governing it are settled.

*Sources: [AI agents threaten traditional payment authentication, warns Wandhöfer](https://www.openbankingexpo.com/news/ai-agents-could-render-traditional-payment-authentication-obsolete-warns-dr-ruth-wandhofer/) — Openbankingexpo*

**Bank of Canada consults on consumer-driven banking accreditation**

*Canada's central bank is designing accreditation guidelines for its open banking regime, offering a live comparison point for European regulators weighing similar frameworks.*

The Bank of Canada has opened a public consultation on accreditation guidelines for participants in its consumer-driven banking framework. The consultation invites stakeholders to comment on how third-party providers should be credentialed and supervised before gaining access to consumer financial data.

Canada's approach places accreditation design with the central bank rather than a dedicated conduct regulator or a market-led body. This contrasts with the UK model, where the FCA oversees open banking authorisation, and with the EU's approach under PSD2 and PSD3, where national competent authorities handle licensing. The consultation's scope and the central bank's direct involvement reflect a conscious decision to treat data access as a systemic infrastructure question rather than purely a consumer protection matter.

The Canadian consultation offers a useful comparison as the EU works toward its own open finance framework and the UK advances its FCA-led roadmap. The accreditation design choices Canada makes, particularly around liability allocation and ongoing supervision, will provide evidence for or against the different institutional models being debated in Europe.

*Sources: [Bank of Canada opens consultation on consumer-driven banking accreditation guidelines](https://tradersunion.com/news/regulators/show/4064542-bank-canada-consultation-banking-guidelines/) — Tradersunion*
